description: I’m Bahrom, and my co-founder Muhammadali and I recently launched Dushanbe Hub. With my background in programming, AI development, and scaling ed-tech platforms, we’re here to expand our horizons, push our limits, and build a project worth bragging about. We are looking for driven teammates with complementary skills in UI/UX design, front-end development, or marketing to help us execute our vision. If you love solving complex problems and want to build something impactful, let’s team up!
summary: Celeste is a health companion for astronauts on long missions, and it solves several problems at once. Body: it combines WHOOP data, hand entered readings and a daily check, and judges everything against what is normal for that astronaut, learned from their own history and overruled by the flight surgeon’s notes and ranges. Mind and isolation: a private wellbeing check, a daily crew mood pulse that stays anonymous, anonymous concerns about a crew mate that reach the doctors, a caring SI that points a person in distress to the flight surgeon, and a family line where relatives sign in with a short code and exchange videos, photos and messages. Safety: a camera on the device detects a possible fall, seizure movement or distress and alerts doctors and crew, and keeps only a written report. Trust: the AI reads the doctor’s notes and health file before it answers, changes only the signed in person’s own data, and shows where every number came from. Distance: live calls exist only near Earth, because a signal takes minutes to reach Mars, so far missions use saved, resumable messages and video, like NASA’s delay tolerant networking. Doctors have their own portal, and a team leader sees the whole crew.
details:
Celeste: health monitoring for astronauts, built for the distance

Long space missions create several health problems at the same time, and Celeste is a crew health companion that addresses each of them. It collects an astronaut’s data from WHOOP, from readings typed in by hand and from a daily check. A flight surgeon sees every astronaut and answers their reports, and a team leader sees how the crew is doing and whether the doctors are responding.

The first problem is distance. A signal takes under a second to reach Earth from the ISS but 4 to 24 minutes from Mars, so a live call there is pointless. Celeste allows live calls and live video only near Earth. Farther out it switches to store and forward: text, voice, photos and normal quality compressed video that are saved first, sent in small pieces, resumed after any break in the link, and played when opened. This follows the principle of NASA’s delay tolerant networking. Relatives use the same system with a short family code instead of an account, and there are no calls with family at all.

The second problem is that population averages do not fit an individual. Celeste learns what is normal for each astronaut from their own last 28 days of data, and a flight surgeon can set their own ranges and write notes that stay in force for a chosen time. The doctor’s input always wins over what the system learned.

The third problem is trust in AI. The SI assistant reads each astronaut’s full dataset before it answers: the health file with allergies and medications, lab files, the doctor’s notes, the normal ranges and the latest readings. It analyses readings every 30 minutes and WHOOP data is pulled every 10 minutes. It can record readings and add allergies when the person asks, and it can propose a day off or a schedule, but the person confirms it. It can only change the data of the signed in person, and only a doctor or team leader may change someone else’s.

The fourth problem is data you cannot trust. Without WHOOP the app shows no numbers, only what the person enters by hand. Zero readings from the strap are treated as sensor gaps, and every number shows where it came from.

The fifth problem is emergencies when nobody is watching. A camera based SI on the device can detect a possible collapse or fall, a person who is not moving, possible seizure movement and distress, and it alerts the doctors and crew mates and keeps escalating if nobody responds. Anyone can also raise an SOS by hand. No video is stored, only a written activity report.

The sixth problem is the body and mind in isolation and microgravity. The app tracks radiation dose separately from space weather context, checks exercise form by camera, adapts the training plan, and lets crew mates raise anonymous concerns and share a daily crew mood pulse.

We used NASA data and resources: the NASA Open Science Data Repository dataset OSD-569 with the Inspiration4 blood counts, the NASA DONKI space weather API for radiation context, and the NASA Human Research Program hazards of radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and environment, on which our Mission tab is built.

We built it with Expo and React Native for one codebase on web and phones, TypeScript, Node.js, Express, SQLite and WebRTC. The AI uses Google Gemini, and the camera features use the open source MediaPipe and face-api.js models, so we trained no model ourselves. We also used the WHOOP API, Resend for email codes, Render for hosting and a domain from the Space Apps offer. We used Claude Code, a super intelligence tool, to help write and test the code and to design the logo, and the demo video and the demo photo in the family demo were generated with code.

The project is creative because it treats distance as a core rule and because it makes the AI accountable to the doctor: the doctor’s notes act as orders that the AI must remember and follow for as long as they are valid.

We considered privacy: face data is stored only as numbers with consent, and voice and video recordings are deleted after a few days. We also considered not inventing data, who may change whose records, and that this is a research prototype and not a medical device.
